Article Title: A Missouri widow changed a family trust and a later amendment gave $220,000 to a beneficiary; after a court ordered repayment, an October 20 ruling dismissed her appeal as too late
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Family trust amendments led to an inheritance dispute

Court ordered Longsdon to repay $220,000

Beneficiaries moved to revive the judgment

Appeals court dismissed the challenge as untimely

A Missouri trust dispute involving a $220,000 payment ended in a procedural setback for the recipient after an appeals court dismissed her challenge because she missed the filing deadline. In its October 20, 2026, ruling, the Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District, held that it lacked jurisdiction to consider Diane Longsdon’s appeal against an order reviving a judgment requiring her to repay the money. According to the court’s opinion, published by Justia, the dispute began with amendments to a family trust created in 1994. The court’s latest decision focused on the appeal deadline, leaving the revived judgment in place rather than reconsidering the original inheritance dispute.Violet M. Steinert and her husband, Fred Steinert Sr., established their living trust on October 12, 1994. Under its original terms, half of the trust’s assets were to be divided equally between Fred’s two sons, Fran Steinert and Fred Steinert Jr. The other half was to be distributed equally among six of Violet’s nieces and nephews. Fred Sr. died in 1998. After his death, Violet amended the trust to remove her stepsons as beneficiaries, despite a provision in the original agreement restricting unilateral amendments after either grantor died.Violet’s final amendment before her death on October 11, 2009, named three additional beneficiaries: Mid-Rivers Christian Church, Diane Longsdon and Paul Rotermund. The amendment allocated $220,000 to Longsdon, $220,000 to the church and $110,000 to Rotermund. The distributions were made in late 2009 and early 2010. The Steinert brothers challenged the amendments in probate court in January 2010. They sought recognition of the original trust, removal of the successor trustee and an accounting of the trust’s assets.In July 2013, the circuit court ruled that the original 1994 trust remained valid. This meant the later amendments were ineffective and the distributions made under them could not stand. On June 4, 2014, the court entered a judgment against Longsdon for the $220,000 she had received, together with statutory interest until payment. An earlier appeal by Longsdon was dismissed in August 2014 after she failed to comply with a special operating rule of the appeals court.The trust proceedings continued. In August 2015, the court assigned the trust’s judgment against Longsdon to the original beneficiaries, approved the final accounting and discharged John Maxwell, who had been appointed successor trustee in 2013. Longsdon appealed, but the appellate court affirmed the judgment. The church and Rotermund later settled their respective claims with the trust concerning the distributions. The judgment against Longsdon remained unpaid, leading the beneficiaries to seek its revival.In August 2025, the beneficiaries asked the circuit court to revive the August 2015 judgment before its 10-year enforcement period expired. Longsdon objected, arguing that the relevant judgment dated to June 2014, rather than August 2015.The distinction was important because the date of the final judgment determined the applicable deadline for seeking revival. On December 19, 2025, the circuit court granted the beneficiaries’ request. It determined that the August 2015 judgment was the final judgment because it resolved the remaining issues, including the assignment of the trust’s claim, approval of the accounting and discharge of the successor trustee. Longsdon filed her notice of appeal on January 20, 2026, challenging the order reviving the judgment.The Missouri Court of Appeals examined when the revival order became final for purposes of calculating the appeal deadline. It considered different approaches adopted by the state’s appellate districts and followed the reasoning of the Southern District. The court held that the special order reviving the judgment became final when it was entered on December 19, 2025. Because Longsdon had not filed an authorised post-trial motion, she had 10 days to file her notice of appeal. The deadline expired on December 29, 2025. Her January 20 filing therefore came too late. The court concluded that it lacked jurisdiction to consider the merits of her challenge and dismissed the appeal.The judges also indicated that Longsdon’s argument about the 10-year revival period appeared unlikely to succeed. The August 2015 judgment had resolved the remaining issues in the trust proceedings, making it the relevant judgment for calculating that period. The October 20 ruling did not revisit the original dispute over Violet’s amendments or reconsider the order requiring repayment. Instead, it left the revived judgment in place because the appeal had not been filed within the required time.
Article Summary: Family trust amendments led to an inheritance dispute. Court ordered Diane Longsdon to repay $220,000.Beneficiaries moved to revive the judgment. Court dismissed the challenge as untimely and left the revived judgment in place rather than reconsidering the original dispute.

Article Title: In 2025, a Wisconsin hiking couple were struck by lightning and Eva revived Nick twice during a 50-minute rescue wait; a year later, they are married, and she is due to receive a lifesaving award
Article Text:
What if we get struck by lightning?

A 50-minute wait for rescuers

Three days in hospital, then a proposal

Recognition for a life-saving act

A hiking trip that nearly cost two people their lives became the beginning of a marriage for a Wisconsin couple, after Eva Broderick performed cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) twice on her boyfriend, Nick, following a lightning strike in August 2025. According to a report by Action News 5, published on October 18, 2026, the couple survived the ordeal, married a year later and are now sharing their story as Eva receives recognition for her actions.The incident took place on August 9, 2025, when Nick took Eva, his then-girlfriend, on a 10-mile hike through Kettle Moraine State Forest in Wisconsin. They were slightly more than two miles from their car when a sudden storm swept in, turning an otherwise enjoyable outing into a desperate struggle to survive. The couple had little opportunity to find shelter and continued along the trail as the rain intensified, according to reporting by Milwaukee television station TMJ4, which first covered their account.As the storm worsened, Eva became increasingly worried. Nick later recalled that she turned to him and asked what would happen if they were struck by lightning. Minutes later, the possibility became reality.Nick remembers hearing a loud boom, after which his memory of the incident stops.Firefighters said lightning struck a nearby tree and the couple were affected by the resulting ground current. Rather than being hit directly by the lightning bolt, they were injured by electricity spreading through the ground after the strike.Eva later described feeling what seemed like electricity in her feet and curling up with her hands over her ears. When she looked towards Nick, she found him lying on his back, with his eyes partly open. He appeared blue and was not breathing, she recalled in an interview with TMJ4.Eva called emergency services and began CPR. However, reaching rescuers proved difficult because her mobile phone signal kept dropping. She also struggled to identify their precise location in the forest, unable to remember the trailhead they had used or exactly which path they had followed.The couple's location created a difficult search for emergency crews. According to Palmyra Fire Rescue Assistant Chief Dan Schiller, the phone's location information placed them somewhere within a broad area of forest rather than identifying a precise spot. Responders had to make their best estimate and search several possible routes. It took around 50 minutes for rescuers to reach the couple on foot after Eva called 911. During that wait, she had to perform CPR on Nick twice, despite having also been affected by the lightning strike herself.Schiller described the circumstances as extraordinary in comments reported by TMJ4. Eva's actions were particularly significant because she was dealing with her own injuries while attempting to keep Nick alive until professional help arrived.The incident also illustrates the difficulty of locating injured hikers in remote areas when phone reception is unreliable. Even when emergency services receive a call, rescuers may have to search a large area on foot if the caller cannot provide an exact location.Nick was taken to hospital after the rescue and spent three days recovering. The effects of the lightning strike did not end when he was discharged: he continued to experience some hearing loss in one ear and tendon-related problems, according to the follow-up report by Action News 5. But the couple's story did not end with the rescue. After leaving the hospital, Nick proposed to Eva. The pair subsequently married in August 2026, almost a year after the incident that had brought them so close to losing each other.Their decision to marry in the same month was deliberate. Nick said they wanted to give August a happier association after the frightening experience of the previous year. Eva has also spoken humorously about the experience. She joked that Nick could not leave her because she had brought him back from death.Eva is being recognised for her actions by the Palmyra Fire Department, which announced that she would receive its Lifesavers Award for helping save Nick's life. Their experience also highlights the importance of knowing CPR and calling emergency services as quickly as possible. The American Heart Association recommends immediate CPR when someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, while emergency dispatchers can provide instructions until professional help arrives.For Eva and Nick, the hike remains a reminder of how quickly conditions outdoors can change. What began as a long walk through the forest ended in a rescue operation, a difficult recovery and, eventually, a wedding. A year later, the couple are looking towards a new chapter, with Eva's actions during those 50 minutes recognised as a decisive part of their survival story.
Article Summary: Eva Broderick performed CPR twice on her boyfriend, Nick, following a lightning strike in August 2025. It took around 50 minutes for rescuers to reach the couple on foot after Eva called 911. Nick was taken to hospital after the rescue and spent three days recovering. After leaving the hospital, Nick proposed to Eva and the pair subsequently married in August 2026. Eva is being recognised for her actions by the Palmyra Fire Department.

Article Title: England rugby legend Lawrence Dallaglio’s World Cup medal sells for £54,000; Eric Cantona’s shorts go under the hammer
Article Text:
England’s historic victory in Sydney

Cantona’s shorts and a World Cup television table

Why sporting memorabilia commands attention

A medal from one of English rugby’s most celebrated nights has changed hands for £54,000, while a pair of shorts associated with football icon Eric Cantona and other sporting keepsakes attracted collectors at an auction in England. The sale, held by sports memorabilia specialist Budds on October 13, featured 332 lots spanning rugby, football, cricket, boxing, golf and tennis, according to the auction house’s official results.The headline item was the 2003 Rugby World Cup winner’s medal belonging to former England captain Lawrence Dallaglio. The silver-gilt medal fetched a hammer price of £54,000, close to the lower end of its pre-sale estimate of £50,000 to £80,000. Twelve items from Dallaglio’s collection sold, with the auction house reporting a combined total of £130,650 including the buyer’s premium.The auction offered a glimpse into the market for sporting memorabilia, where objects associated with defining victories can carry a value that extends well beyond their material worth.The medal commemorates England’s 20-17 victory over Australia in the Rugby World Cup final on November 22, 2003.Played in Sydney, the match went into extra time before Jonny Wilkinson’s famous drop goal secured England’s first men’s Rugby World Cup title. Dallaglio, who captained England during his career, was part of the squad that lifted the trophy.The medal was made of silver-gilt and remained in its original fitted case, complete with a green and blue ribbon. Its reverse listed the Australian cities that hosted matches during the tournament, according to Budds’ description. The object therefore preserved a tangible connection to a landmark moment in English rugby history.Dallaglio’s collection included several other reminders of his playing career. His red British and Irish Lions cap sold for £11,000, while his England international cap fetched £8,000. Both attracted strong bidding, with the Lions cap achieving twice the upper end of its pre-sale estimate. His purple World Rugby Hall of Fame cap, estimated at £500 to £800, sold for £2,400.His 2003 Six Nations Championship winners’ medal fetched £7,500, while the medal he received as a runner-up at the 2007 Rugby World Cup sold for £5,000. A medal from the 2004 Heineken Cup final, won with Wasps, brought £4,400. Five pewter tankards from different points in his career and associated sporting activities sold for £1,600.However, not every item found a buyer. Budds’ catalogue listed several other Dallaglio medals and awards that failed to meet their reserves, demonstrating that an association with a famous athlete does not guarantee a sale at every price.The auction extended well beyond rugby. Among its football-related curiosities were shorts associated with Eric Cantona, the former Manchester United forward whose playing career and outspoken personality made him one of the Premier League’s most recognisable figures. The collection also included shirts associated with players such as Harry Kane, alongside memorabilia from other generations of football.Another unusual lot was the table used by presenters in the BBC television studio during the 1998 FIFA World Cup. Formerly owned by singer Robbie Williams , it sold for £800 after attracting interest from bidders in Britain and the United States, The Guardian reported. The table offered a different kind of sporting connection: rather than coming from the pitch, it was associated with the television coverage through which millions followed the tournament.The auction also included a 2008-09 Manchester United shirt associated with Cristiano Ronaldo, which sold for £6,000. A shirt worn by Ole Gunnar Solskjaer during the 1999-2000 season fetched £2,200, while a signed Arsenal shirt associated with Ray Parlour sold for £4,000. These results illustrated the range of items attracting collectors, from match-related clothing to objects connected with memorable teams and seasons.The Dallaglio auction comes amid a wider boom in high-value sports collectables. In its October 16 report, The Guardian highlighted the growing market for match-worn football shirts and other objects associated with iconic sporting moments, noting that international buyers and online bidding have widened the pool of potential collectors.Some sales operate on a vastly different scale. A jersey worn by basketball legend Michael Jordan during the 1998 NBA Finals sold for more than £10 million in October 2026, according to the newspaper. In football, the shirt Diego Maradona wore during Argentina’s 1986 World Cup quarter-final against England was sold for more than £7 million in 2022.Dallaglio’s medal belongs to a different price bracket, but its significance is rooted in the same connection between an object and a defining sporting achievement. For collectors, the appeal lies not simply in the metal, fabric or craftsmanship, but in the history attached to it.The sale also comes against a difficult financial backdrop for the former England captain. The Guardian reported that Dallaglio had been declared bankrupt a year earlier, while The Telegraph, in a report republished by Yahoo Sports, linked the sale of his memorabilia to his financial circumstances.Ultimately, the £54,000 hammer price placed a piece of England’s 2003 triumph in a new owner’s hands. The auction’s other lots, from Cantona-associated shorts to a television studio table, showed how sporting history can survive in objects that might otherwise appear ordinary, becoming valuable to those who want to own a fragment of the game’s past.
Article Summary: The medal commemorates England’s 20-17 victory over Australia in the Rugby World Cup final on November 22, 2003. The silver-gilt medal fetched a hammer price of £54,000, close to the lower end of its pre-sale estimate of £50,000 to £80,000. The auction offered a glimpse into the market for sporting memorabilia.

Article Title: An Australian designer develops hempcrete tiles to recreate tree hollows and rocky crevices; shelters aim to help threatened wildlife, including eastern quolls and ringtail possums
Article Text:
How hempcrete tiles recreate tree hollows and rocky crevices

Why Australia's wildlife needs alternative shelters

Which animals could benefit from Bush Cradle?

Eastern quolls

Ringtail possums

Other native wildlife

Early field observations offer an encouraging sign

Who developed Bush Cradle?

What comes next for the project?

Australian designer Xavier Earls has developed Bush Cradle, a modular wildlife habitat system made from hempcrete tiles that mimic natural shelters such as tree hollows, fallen logs and rocky crevices. The system is designed to help conservationists create customised refuges for native animals facing habitat loss. Its four interlocking tile designs can be assembled into different configurations, including tree hollows and ground dens, with entrances tailored to individual species. The project aims to address the shortage of natural shelter for wildlife, including eastern quolls and ringtail possums. In an encouraging early observation, ringtail possums reportedly used a prototype overnight, offering an initial indication of the design's potential.Bush Cradle uses four tile shapes connected through a slot-and-pin mechanism, allowing shelters to be assembled, dismantled and rearranged by hand without conventional tools. This makes it possible to adapt their configurations to different species and environments.The tiles are made from fibrous hempcrete, chosen for its insulating properties. Their manufacture combines 3D printing and casting, with lightweight printed frames placed inside moulds before hempcrete is poured in and left to cure.Laser-cut wooden entrance pieces allow openings to be customised for different animals.According to Earls' project description, the developed tiles weigh approximately 200 grams each, compared with early prototypes that weighed more than one kilogram. The modular design also allows individual components to be repaired or replaced without discarding an entire shelter.Natural features such as tree hollows, fallen logs and rocky crevices provide essential places for animals to rest, nest, hide from predators and raise their young. However, land clearing, development and habitat degradation are reducing the availability of these refuges.Tree hollows are particularly important for many native species, but they can take hundreds of years to form naturally. When mature trees disappear, the animals that depend on their hollows can lose essential shelter long before replacement habitats develop.Bush Cradle offers a potential way to bridge this gap by allowing conservationists to construct artificial refuges suited to particular species and landscapes. Its adaptable components provide an alternative to conventional nest boxes, which are often designed for a specific purpose.The system is intended to accommodate different native Australian animals by allowing shelters to be tailored to their habitat requirements.: These spotted, nocturnal marsupials use dens and other sheltered spaces. Bush Cradle can be configured to mimic hollow logs and ground refuges, with entrances and chambers adapted to their needs.: These tree-dwelling marsupials need protected places to rest. A Bush Cradle prototype installed in a tree was reportedly occupied by wild ringtail possums overnight.: Earls has identified potential applications for pygmy possums, reptiles, endangered skinks and microbats. Different configurations could accommodate their varying entrance sizes and shelter requirements.Trail-camera footage reportedly recorded ringtail possums using a Bush Cradle prototype installed in a tree overnight. The observation provided an early indication that the structure could serve as a usable refuge beyond the design studio.However, a single observation cannot establish whether the shelters improve long-term survival, breeding success or population recovery. Further monitoring would be needed to determine how consistently different species use the structures and how well they perform under varying weather conditions.Earls created Bush Cradle as his final-year industrial design project at Monash University in Australia. His work combines ecological research, digital modelling, 3D printing and material experimentation to explore how design could help address habitat loss.An internship at Reef Design Lab helped him explore how digital fabrication and casting could be combined to produce habitat structures. Earls now works full-time at the organisation, continuing to investigate how design can support ecosystems.Bush Cradle received a Best in Class Award in the Next Gen category at the 2026 Australian Good Design Awards, according to Monash University. The recognition highlighted the project's approach to combining industrial design with wildlife conservation.Earls aims to establish a network of conservationists who can use Bush Cradle to create customised wildlife refuges in Australia and potentially elsewhere. The project has also attracted interest for possible use in restoring habitat for endangered skinks and microbats in mining-affected areas of northern Queensland.The long-term ambition is to make artificial habitat creation more accessible, allowing conservationists to respond to the requirements of different species rather than relying on a single shelter design.
Article Summary: Australian designer Xavier Earls has developed a modular wildlife habitat system made from hempcrete tiles. The system is designed to help conservationists create customised refuges for native animals facing habitat loss. Its four interlocking tile designs can be assembled into different configurations, including tree hollows and ground dens, with entrances tailored to individual species.

Article Title: Florida scientists tracked 142 invasive Burmese pythons for 20 years and found that all four expelled tracking devices came from pregnant females
Article Text:
PC: Case report: observations on expulsionsfrom 20 years of radiotransmitter implantationin adult Burmese pythons

How many Burmese python tracking devices were expelled in Florida

PC: Case report: observations on expulsionsfrom 20 years of radiotransmitter implantationin adult Burmese pythons

How did four Burmese pythons lose their implanted tracking devices

Why might pregnant Burmese pythons be more likely to expel devices

Scientists tracking invasive Burmese pythons in southern Florida recorded four cases of implanted tracking devices being expelled during a study spanning 2005 to 2024. The study examined 305 transmitters implanted in 142 adult snakes across Big Cypress National Preserve and Everglades National Park. According to the report published in the Journal of Animal Biotelemetry, titled ‘ Case report: observations on expulsions from 20 years of radiotransmitter implantation in adult Burmese pythons ’, the research found that all four expulsions involved gravid females with intramuscularly implanted transmitters. No transmitter-related deaths were observed. The researchers also examined whether reproduction and implantation methods could influence device retention, noting that both surgical techniques were effective for monitoring adult pythons.Of the 305 transmitters implanted during the study, 221 were placed intramuscularly, while 84 were positioned inside the coelomic cavity. The researchers reported that four transmitters were expelled, representing 1.3% of the total. All four cases involved intramuscularly implanted transmitters in gravid females, meaning females carrying developing eggs. No transmitter-related deaths were observed among the study animals.The four expulsions occurred in females that had received their implants in late January or early February, during the breeding season, which runs from December to March. The devices were expelled before the females laid their eggs. The researchers recorded the expulsions between 57 and 111 days after surgery, with a reported mean of 101 days. The paper’s abstract summarised the findings: “Overall, 98.7% of transmitters were retained, with a 1.3% expulsion rate (n = 4 transmitters). ” The researchers also reported that the four cases occurred among 13 gravid females in the relevant group, while other gravid females retained their transmitters and subsequently laid clutches of eggs.The paper describes four individual cases involving female pythons in Big Cypress National Preserve. In the first case, a female measuring 414 centimetres in snout-to-vent length and weighing 42 kilograms received two transmitters on 26 January 2006. When researchers recaptured her on 17 May that year, she had a clutch of 46 eggs, and one transmitter was lying on the ground nearby. Both devices had been detected at her previous location two days earlier. An examination found no abscesses or skin wounds, leaving the mechanism of expulsion unknown. The researchers recorded the event 111 days after surgery.The other three cases involved females implanted in January or February 2022. In one case, a female measuring 450 centimetres and weighing 81.2 kilograms had a transmitter visible through an open skin abscess on 1 April, approximately 80 days after implantation. The animal was removed from the field for surgery as the abscess enlarged. A replacement transmitter was implanted on 29 April, and the female laid 81 eggs on 23 May. In the fourth case, a female measuring 441 centimetres and weighing 73.6 kilograms had a transmitter visible through an open abscess on 1 April, 57 days after surgery. The transmitter was replaced on 29 April, and the python laid 96 eggs between 21 and 23 May. The researchers also documented an earlier case in which a transmitter was partially expelled through an open skin abscess 155 days after surgery. These observations show that the circumstances surrounding expulsion differed between individual snakes, including whether an abscess or visible wound was present.The researchers said the low expulsion rate indicated that both intramuscular and coelomic implantation techniques were effective for monitoring adult Burmese pythons. However, they identified a possible association between transmitter expulsion and the reproductive status of females. In their discussion, they wrote: “This suggests that some gravid females may be at a higher risk for expelling transmitters, compared to males or non-gravid females. ” They proposed that changes associated with reproduction, including possible changes in immune response and pressure within the body cavity, might contribute to the risk. These explanations were presented as possibilities rather than established causes.The study also found that all four expelled devices had been implanted intramuscularly. The authors suggested that placing transmitters inside the coelomic cavity might reduce the risk of expulsion in gravid females, but stressed that the number of recorded cases was small. They noted that the cause of expulsion could involve abscess formation at the incision site rather than the timing of implantation relative to egg-laying. Their conclusion stated: “We observed no mortality related to transmitter implantation and few instances of transmitter expulsion, indicating that both intramuscular and coelomic implantation techniques are effective for monitoring adult pythons in the wild.” The authors added that their findings may inform research on other large-bodied snake populations where radiotransmitter implantation is appropriate and feasible.
Article Summary: Scientists tracking invasive Burmese pythons in southern Florida recorded four cases of implanted tracking devices being expelled during a study spanning 2005 to 2024. Study examined 305 transmitters implanted in 142 adult snakes across Big Cypress National Preserve and Everglades National Park. All four cases involved intramuscularly implanted transmitters in gravid females, meaning females carrying developing eggs. The devices were expelled before the females laid their eggs.

Article Title: In 2019, Chance the Rapper’s charity selected a Chicago youth therapy programme for a $100,000 grant, backing three years of support including safe summer experiences for children affected by violence
Article Text:
Making mental health support more accessible

Creating safe spaces beyond traditional therapy

Chance the Rapper’s philanthropic work in Chicago extended beyond education, with his nonprofit organisation SocialWorks directing funding towards mental health services for communities that often struggle to access care. One of its beneficiaries was Under the Rainbow, a youth therapy programme run by Sinai Health System that works with children, adolescents and their families affected by trauma and community violence. Based on reporting by SocialWorks, alongside coverage by ABC News and CBS News on Chance the Rapper’s mental health philanthropy, the programme was selected in December 2019 as one of six recipients of SocialWorks’ My State of Mind initiative, which was designed to improve access to mental health support and encourage more open conversations about emotional well-being. The grant was meant to fund services for three years, including therapeutic summer camps and activities where young people and their families could connect in a safe environment outside traditional clinical settings. Continued support was especially important because nearly 85 per cent of young people in Under the Rainbow were reported to have PTSD, and all had experienced community violence.The grant formed part of a wider commitment announced by Chance the Rapper, whose real name is Chancelor Bennett, in October 2018.Through SocialWorks, he pledged $1 million towards mental health services in Chicago, with six providers in Cook County set to receive grants of $100,000 each.As reported by ABC News and CBS News at the time, the initiative sought to address barriers to mental health care and connect residents with appropriate services. My State of Mind was developed as part of that effort, with a focus on helping people find wellness resources and making mental health support easier to navigate.The programme also reflected SocialWorks’ broader community-focused approach. Founded to empower young people through arts, education and civic engagement, the organisation has pursued projects intended to expand opportunities for Chicago residents, particularly young people from underserved communities.Under the Rainbow’s selection reflected the importance of combining professional mental health care with experiences that help families build trust and emotional connections. For children exposed to violence, support can extend beyond appointments with therapists to include environments where they can feel safe, participate in activities and connect with others facing similar challenges.The funding was expected to help Under the Rainbow continue offering activities such as therapeutic summer camps, giving children and families opportunities to engage in healing outside the traditional therapy room. For Sinai Health System, the partnership offered a way to sustain services for young people dealing with difficult experiences while broadening the ways they could access support. SocialWorks, meanwhile, viewed the grants as an opportunity to back organisations that were already connected to their communities and were approaching mental health care through a combination of clinical treatment and community-based programmes.The initiative highlighted a central challenge in youth mental health: access to care is not only about the availability of professional services, but also about creating environments where seeking help feels acceptable and safe.By supporting Under the Rainbow, SocialWorks aimed to help preserve a programme that addressed trauma while giving young people and their families opportunities to connect, recover and build resilience. The partnership was one part of Chance the Rapper’s wider effort to invest in Chicago communities through philanthropy, with mental health support placed alongside education and youth development as areas requiring long-term attention.
Article Summary: Chance the Rapper pledged $1 million towards mental health services in Chicago in October 2018. His nonprofit organisation, SocialWorks, helped develop the My State of Mind initiative. One of its beneficiaries was Under the Rainbow, a youth therapy programme that works with children, adolescents and their families affected by trauma and community violence. The grant was meant to fund services for three years, including therapeutic summer camps and activities.

Article Title: Kim Jong Un photos released to dismiss rumours of coma, takeover by sister
Article Text:
Kim Jong Un inspects pink shoe, women’s coats as death rumours grip North Korea

How the death rumours began

Claims of Chinese troop deployment

What is known about Kim's health?

North Korean supreme leader Kim Jong Un has resurfaced in photographs released by state media, inspecting children's footwear and women's clothing, after unverified claims circulated online that he had died from a brain haemorrhage.The photographs, published by North Korea's official media on Monday, show Kim examining footwear, gesturing towards officials and inspecting coats at a garment and footwear exhibition. The images emerged amid a wave of social media speculation about the 42-year-old leader's health and the possibility of a succession crisis in the secretive country, the New York Post reported.According to North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency, Kim toured the exhibition on Monday. However, the photographs have not been independently authenticated, and it remains unclear precisely when they were taken.One image shows Kim bending forward to inspect a small pink shoe held by a woman. In another, he gestures with his arms outstretched as he appears to address an official. A third photograph captures him reaching towards the sleeve of a woman's coat displayed on a mannequin.The speculation gathered pace after Wanjun Xie, a US-based Chinese dissident associated with the China Democracy Party, posted a series of claims on X alleging that Kim had died and that his sister, Kim Yo Jong , had taken control of the country.In a post on Monday, Xie wrote: "Rumours of the death of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un have been circulating online for days, but Kim Jong Un has not yet made a public appearance to deny them. This indirectly confirms that the rumours of Kim Jong Un's death are likely true. Furthermore, it is rumoured that after Kim Jong-un's death, the North Korean regime has not been transferred to his daughter Kim Ju-ae, but is currently in the hands of his sister Kim Yo-jong."After assuming power, Kim Yo-jong immediately activated loudspeaker broadcasts to South Korea and fired 201 warning shots. She also warned South Korea that North Korea was considering a comprehensive upgrade of its tactical strike capabilities. This sudden intensification of threats against South Korea is clearly aimed at strengthening her control over the North Korean military and consolidating her power through strong external threats. This indirectly confirms the rumors that Kim Jong-un is dead and that Kim Yo-jong is currently in control of the regime; these rumors are likely true."The New York Post reported that Xie's claims began gaining traction on Sunday. However, the allegations have not been supported by medical records, identifiable witnesses or other independently verifiable evidence.In another post on Sunday, Xie claimed that Kim had suffered a severe cerebral haemorrhage, fallen into a coma and been transferred to Beijing for emergency treatment. He alleged that a team of specialists from Peking Union Medical College Hospital had travelled to North Korea before Kim was moved to China."It is rumoured that recently, Kim Jong-un, General Secretary of the Workers' Party of Korea and Supreme Leader of North Korea, suffered a severe cerebral haemorrhage and fell into a coma. Although a team of medical experts from Peking Union Medical College Hospital was dispatched to North Korea to assist in his treatment, the poor medical conditions in North Korea forced Kim Jong-un to be transferred to Peking Union Medical College Hospital for emergency treatment. However, due to the severity of his condition and the fact that the optimal window for treatment had passed, Kim Jong-un succumbed to his injuries and died. His body has been secretly transported back to North Korea, and the news of his death is being kept under wraps."Xie further alleged that Kim's body had been secretly returned to North Korea and that authorities were concealing news of his death. He also claimed that Chinese troops had been deployed to Pyongyang amid fears of a succession crisis.In a separate post, he wrote: "It is said that on October 17, Peking Union Medical College Hospital dispatched a team of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular medical experts to North Korea to participate in the rescue of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, who was in critical condition."Xie's posts also fuelled speculation about a possible power struggle involving Kim's daughter, Kim Ju-ae, and his sister, Kim Yo Jong. He claimed that China had sent 9,000 troops to Pyongyang to help stabilise the situation.The claims of Kim's death, a Chinese troop deployment and a possible succession crisis remain unverified. North Korean authorities have not explicitly addressed the death reports.Kim's health has long been the subject of international speculation. The New York Post reported that South Korea's National Intelligence Service told lawmakers on September 30 that Kim weighed approximately 140 kilograms (309 pounds) and faced an elevated risk of cardiovascular disease because of severe obesity.However, the agency reportedly detected no significant signs of ill health, pointing to Kim's ability to run up stairs during an inspection of a naval destroyer.The latest rumours echo a false alarm in 2020, when Ji Seong-ho, a North Korean defector who later became a South Korean lawmaker, claimed he was "99%" certain that Kim had died following cardiovascular surgery. Kim subsequently appeared in public, and Ji apologised for making the erroneous claim.The New York Post said it had sought comment from the governments of North Korea and China, as well as Peking Union Medical College Hospital.
Article Summary: North Korean supreme leader Kim Jong Un has resurfaced in photographs released by state media. The images emerged amid a wave of social media speculation about the 42-year-old leader's health and the possibility of a succession crisis. Unverified claims circulated online that he had died from a brain haemorrhage.

Article Title: Russia’s digital Achilles’ heel? How Ukraine data centre strikes are disrupting daily life
Article Text:
Ukraine hits Russia’s tech nerve centre as data outages disrupt daily life (Representative Image)

Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian data centres have disrupted banking, taxi services, food deliveries and digital access to homes, exposing the vulnerability of services used by millions of Russians. This comes as Kyiv expands its campaign against Moscow’s technology infrastructure.The attacks, carried out over several days in October, targeted data centres operated by Yandex, Russia’s largest technology company, followed by a facility owned by Sberbank, the country’s largest bank. A data centre belonging to technology group VK was also reportedly targeted.Yandex, often described as “Russia’s Google”, provides search, email, navigation, music, ride-hailing, food delivery, cloud computing and digital payment services.Connectivity to the Yandex Cloud platform fell to around 30 per cent of normal levels following the October 8-11 strikes, The Moscow times reported, quoting internet monitoring group NetBlocks.Disruptions also affected third-party businesses that depend on its infrastructure, with users reporting problems accessing files, ordering taxis and entering residential buildings after digital keys stopped working.Yandex confirmed that one data centre had sustained significant damage, another had been shut down, and a third had suffered infrastructure disruptions.Although access to Yandex Pay was subsequently restored, several people reported that the service displayed an incorrect account balance.According to The Moscow Times, Yandex Pay remained only partially operational as of Monday, displaying a reassurance to users in place of the earlier error message: “Your money is safe. Some features are unavailable. Our engineers are working to get everything up and running again.”State agencies and private businesses relying on Yandex infrastructure, including dating apps and access systems for residential complexes and smart homes, also faced disruptions, The Moscow Times reported.Taxi drivers were also affected. Three drivers told NBC News they could not track their earnings or withdraw their money during the outage. One said the application had displayed error messages and, at times, dispatched multiple cars for a single customer.On October 14, Ukrainian drones struck a Sberbank data centre in the Saratov region. However, the bank said its systems remained operational.“We confirm that the data processing centre was attacked. At the same time, all of Sberbank's systems and services are operating normally and without disruption,” Alexander Vedyakhin, Sberbank’s first deputy CEO told Reuters.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the government was discussing Yandex’s difficulties but that it was too early to assess whether users had suffered financial losses. Russia’s digital development minister Maksut Shadayev said officials were working with the defence ministry on measures to protect data centres, according to The Moscow Times.Ukraine has described the strikes as retaliation for Russian attacks on its own digital infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Moscow of trying to “leave Ukrainians without the internet”.The attacks have exposed the risks posed by Russia’s reliance on a relatively small number of major technology providers.Meanwhile, Russia has also intensified attacks on Ukraine’s digital and energy infrastructure. However, Russian data centres were potentially more vulnerable because many are concentrated in a handful of large facilities, whereas Ukraine’s are more widely dispersed. A strike on a single Russian facility can therefore disrupt services spanning payments, transport and internet access.
Article Summary: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian data centres have disrupted banking, taxi services, food deliveries and digital access to homes. This comes as Kyiv expands its campaign against Moscow’s technology infrastructure. The attacks, carried out over several days in October, targeted data centres operated by Yandex.

Article Title: Explosion, fuel leak: Two Syrian pipelines damaged in fresh blow to war-hit energy network
Article Text:
Security forces of Syria's Interior Ministry guard the al-Omar oil field, the country's largest by area and production

Two pipelines carrying gas and petroleum products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria on Thursday, with one explosion triggering a fire and another causing a fuel leak, Syrian state media reported.According to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), citing the state-owned Syrian Petroleum Company, an explosion struck the Jbessa gas pipeline in Hasakah province, while a separate leak was detected on the Baniyas-Homs petroleum-products pipeline near Homs.The explosion struck the Jbessa gas export pipeline in the al-Arabidi area of Hasakah province, setting the pipeline on fire. Emergency teams isolated the damaged section and shut valves to contain the blaze.The Syrian Petroleum Company described the incident as sabotage. Officials said alternative arrangements would maintain gas supplies to power stations during repairs, while domestic gas supplies remained unaffected.In a separate incident, a hole was discovered in the Baniyas-Homs pipeline in the Hadida area west of Homs, causing a leak of petroleum products. Emergency and technical teams were deployed to contain the leak and isolate the damaged section.Al Jazeera, citing Syrian state media, reported that the damage to the Baniyas-Homs pipeline was believed to be linked to an attempted fuel theft. The initial reports did not confirm the cause or identify those responsible.The incidents come amid a series of disruptions to Syria’s energy infrastructure. Earlier in October, an oil pipeline near Tal Hamis in Hasakah province was damaged in what the Syrian Petroleum Company described as sabotage.Syria is working to rebuild its oil and gas infrastructure after years of conflict, restoring production in northeastern oilfields and reconnecting them with processing facilities and refineries in Homs and Baniyas.In January 2026, the Syrian Petroleum Company began pumping raw gas from the Jbessa fields in Hasakah to the Furqlus gas plant in Homs countryside at around 1.2 million cubic metres per day to support electricity generation.The second damaged pipeline, connecting Baniyas on the Mediterranean coast to Homs, transports petroleum products between two important energy centres. The Baniyas refinery is undergoing an overhaul aimed at increasing its processing capacity from around 80,000 to 130,000 barrels per day.Syria has also undertaken emergency pipeline repairs and plans to expand its transportation network. A September 2026 analysis by the Baker Institute for Public Policy reported that the Syrian Petroleum Company was repairing existing infrastructure and planning a heavy-crude pipeline linking northeastern oilfields to the Baniyas refinery.
Article Summary: Two pipelines carrying gas and petroleum products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria on Thursday. One explosion struck the Jbessa gas export pipeline in the al-Arabidi area of Hasakah province, setting the pipeline on fire. Emergency teams isolated the damaged section and shut valves to contain the blaze. A separate leak was detected on the Baniyas-Homs petroleum-products pipeline near Homs.

Article Title: 'Quiet, quiet, are you a sick person?' Trumps snaps at reporter at White House; watch
Article Text:
Trump snaps at Independent reporter Andrew Feinberg, asking, “Are you a sick person?” during an Oval Office exchange

US President Donald Trump snapped at a reported in the Oval Office on Tuesday (local time), repeatedly telling him to be “quiet” before asking, “What’s wrong with you? Are you a sick person?”The exchange took place during an event where Trump and Vice President JD Vance discussed a new whistleblower programme offering rewards of up to $30,000 for reporting alleged fraud.The Independent reporter Andrew Feinberg questioned the rationale behind the proposal, pointing out that an existing law already allows whistleblowers to receive a share of funds recovered by the government.According to Feinberg’s account in The Independent, Trump responded to his question by saying, “Because it’s a lot of money.”As he appeared to begin asking about changes to East Potomac Park, which include a new golf course, saying, “On the golf course, sir, you own a lot of golf cour—”“Wait, wait, wait, wait,” Trump interrupted before telling the reporter, “Quiet, quiet.”“What’s wrong with you? Are you a sick person?” Trump asked. “Not that I know of, sir,” Feinberg replied.Feinberg said Vance intervened during the exchange, calling his question “dishonest” and arguing that certain types of fraud fell outside the scope of the False Claims Act. Trump then asked the reporter, “Who are you?” despite Feinberg having identified himself earlier.Vice President JD Vance later took a swipe at Feinberg on X, sharing a clip of the exchange and writing: “President Donald J Trump eviscerates imbecile ‘journalist’ Andrew Feinberg for misbehaving in the Oval Office:”Responding to Vance’s post, Feinberg said, “if you’re going to insult me at least have the guts to tag my account.”Trump has frequently clashed with journalists during his two terms in office.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump snapped at a reported in the Oval Office on Tuesday (local time) He repeatedly told the reporter to be "quiet" before asking, "What's wrong with you? Are you a sick person?” The exchange took place during an event where Trump and Vice President JD Vance discussed a new whistleblower programme.

Article Title: Three siblings, aged 10, 12 and 13, rescued teenagers from a sinking boat in Tennessee; a thunderstorm hit shortly after the rescue
Article Text:
PC: ARLnow

How three siblings rescued teenagers from a sinking boat in Tennessee

How did the Jackson siblings help rescue the stranded teenagers

Siblings’ scouting skills help them rescue teenagers before a thunderstorm

Three siblings aged 10, 12 and 13 helped rescue four teenagers from a sinking boat on Boone Lake in rural Tennessee after the vessel struck a rock and began taking on water. Declan, Cormac and Elsa Jackson were visiting their grandparents when they heard calls for help as storm clouds gathered. Declan and Elsa spotted the teenagers waving for assistance while fishing, prompting Declan to alert their grandparents. Cormac then took the family’s Pond Prowler fishing boat towards the stranded group, helping bring them to safety before a heavy thunderstorm struck the area.Declan and Elsa were fishing when they heard a foghorn and spotted teenagers waving for help. Declan recalled seeing them shouting, “Help us! Help us!” He ran to alert their grandparents while his siblings prepared to assist using their grandparents’ Pond Prowler fishing boat. According to a 911 audio recording reviewed by ARLnow, four teenagers had struck a rock in the middle of the lake, and their boat was flooding. The water had risen above the boat’s battery, leaving the teenagers worried about the risk of electrocution.Cormac steered the family’s fishing boat towards the stranded teenagers. When they all tried to board at once, he explained that he could take only one person at a time because he was concerned about overloading the vessel.His first passenger was an extremely distressed girl, according to their mother, Laura Jackson. She recalled the girl saying she had feared she would die. Cormac reassured her by referring to the life-saving merit badge he had recently earned through scouting.The Jackson siblings rescued another teenager and a bag containing electronics before the owner of a nearby marina arrived to help the remaining teenagers. A pontoon boat also stopped at the scene, although its owner was initially hesitant to take the teenagers aboard.Laura Jackson explained that the accident happened far from shore, where reaching land by swimming would have required considerable strength. The rural location also meant emergency services took about half an hour to arrive.According to ARLnow, a heavy thunderstorm struck shortly after the last teenager had been brought to safety. The siblings’ actions came as conditions around the lake were deteriorating and the damaged boat continued to sink.Laura Jackson praised her children for applying their scouting skills during the emergency. “I couldn’t be prouder of my children,” she told ARLnow, crediting their courage, teamwork and willingness to help others. Declan is a Cub Scout, Cormac is a First Class Scout, and Elsa is a Life Scout in Boy Scouts and a Silver Award Girl Scout.
Article Summary: Three siblings aged 10, 12 and 13 helped rescue four teenagers from a sinking boat on Boone Lake in rural Tennessee. Declan, Cormac and Elsa Jackson were visiting their grandparents when they heard calls for help. Cormac steered the family’s Pond Prowler fishing boat towards the stranded group, helping bring them to safety.

NEW DELHI: Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, the chief of pro-Khalistan outfit Sikhs for Justice, has claimed to have received an intimation from FBI, warning him about an imminent, fresh theat to his life. On October 7, the RCMP also issued a threat-to-life warning to Avtar Singh Pannu, an American Khalistan Referendum coordinator visiting Edmonton to organize the October 18 vote.“I may not live to see Khalistan, but I am determined that the next generation of Sikhs will live in a free Punjab. On October 18, Edmonton will write another chapter in the struggle for Punjab’s liberation from Indian occupation," Pannun said in his statement shared with TOI.SFJ said it will be going ahead with its October 18 Khalistan Referendum plans.

Article Title: In 2014, a North Dakota couple took over a family farm with drained wetlands; after 83 acres were restored, pelicans, ducks and pollinators appeared
Article Text:
The Kunz property sits in an area of the northern Great Plains called the Prairie Pothole Region | Wikimedia Commons

Why so many North Dakota wetlands were drained

The couple chose a long-term conservation agreement

Sharp-tailed grouse, Prairie Pothole Region | Wikimedia Commons

Pelicans were among the returning wildlife

Chad and Jennifer Kunz took over their family property in central North Dakota in 2014, and found that a lot of its potential wetland habitat had been altered by decades of agricultural drainage. The couple decided to restore the land rather than continue trying to farm every acre, and by the time the US Fish and Wildlife Service documented their work, 83 acres of drained wetlands had been restored, and the couple had begun seeing pelicans, ducks, pollinators and other wildlife on the property.The couple moved into a basic cabin without running water or a bathroom, according to the US Fish and Wildlife Service's account of the project , and their first challenge was to find a practical way to manage the property while also protecting its remaining grasslands and rebuilding its wetlands.The Kunz property sits in an area of the northern Great Plains called the Prairie Pothole Region, which is known for its numerous shallow wetlands, and these depressions hold water at different times of the year and provide breeding and feeding habitat for waterfowl and other wildlife. Agricultural expansion changed a big part of the landscapes during the 20th century, wherein farmers drained wetlands to create additional cropland, which was encouraged by government programmes that used to once supported drainage as part of agricultural development.The 1985 Farm Bill introduced federal wetland conservation provisions that are commonly linked with the Swampbuster programme, and these provisions discourage the conversion of wetlands for agricultural production under specified conditions. The US Department of Agriculture's Natural Resources Conservation Service also operates conservation programmes that help landowners restore and protect wetlands, with its Agricultural Conservation Easement Program, for example, providing assistance for restoring and enhancing eligible wetlands. The agency identifies the potential benefits as wildlife habitat, improved water quality, groundwater recharge and reduced flood risk.Chad's father enrolled the land in the federal Conservation Reserve Program in 1987, and that Program supports conservation practices on agricultural land through arrangements that can protect grasslands and other environmentally sensitive areas. In 2018, the couple signed a grassland and wetland easement with the US Fish and Wildlife Service, with the agreement being intended to protect the land permanently rather than rely on a shorter-term conservation contract.Restoration work began in 2019, and assistance was provided by the federal wildlife agency and funding partners, including the North Dakota Natural Resources Trust. The couple also made changes to the farm's infrastructure to support grazing, and installed more than nine miles of fencing, a cattle water well and three watering tanks. Chad and Jennifer leased the land to cattle producers and used grazing as an alternative to cultivating areas that were difficult to farm, while telling the US Fish and Wildlife Service that the arrangement made financial sense for their operation.Jennifer Kunz reported that flowering plants had spread through areas that used to hold murky water and sediment earlier, and also observed insects, pollinators and ducks. Pelicans were among the more notable arrivals, since their presence suggested that the restored wetland areas were supporting aquatic life, although the agency's account did not provide a formal wildlife population survey or quantify how many birds had returned. The couple also believed that they had identified a sharp-tailed grouse breeding display site, known as a lek, and male sharp-tailed grouse gather at these sites during the breeding season to perform courtship displays.Restored wetlands hold surface water and help replenish groundwater, and the Kunz family reported improvements in water storage on their property, which they linked to the needs of their grazing operation. The couple also enrolled the land in North Dakota's Private Land Open To Sportsmen programme, which provides public hunting access on participating private properties.
Article Summary: Chad and Jennifer Kunz took over their family property in central North Dakota in 2014. They found that a lot of its potential wetland habitat had been altered by decades of agricultural drainage. The couple decided to restore the land rather than continue trying to farm every acre. They signed a long-term conservation agreement with the US Fish and Wildlife Service.

Article Title: In 2017, Kaley Cuoco bought a 40-acre California ranch for $4.99 million; nine years later, the Big Bang Theory star's property has become a refuge for rescued horses, cows, goats, pigs and other anim
Article Text:
Cuoco spends time at the ranch with partner Tom Pelphrey and their daughter Matilda. (Photo: Instagram/Cuoco)

Horse ranch becomes home for different animals

Why older rescued animals are especially important to her

Ranch became part of her daughter's childhood

Animal Cuoco still hopes to rescue

When Kaley Cuoco purchased a 40-acre property in California for $4.99 million in 2017, it already had facilities for keeping horses. Nine years later, the ranch has become a refuge for rescued animals, including horses, cows, goats, pigs, donkeys and birds. The actress, who became widely known for playing Penny in The Big Bang Theory, has spent years developing the property to accommodate animals that need a home.Located in Thousand Oaks, northwest of Los Angeles, the ranch was originally designed for people interested in horse riding and keeping horses. According to Realtor.com, the property lies in the foothills of the Santa Monica Mountains and includes a three-bedroom, 2,720-square-foot house. It was advertised as an equestrian estate when Cuoco bought it, with a barn and arenas already available.But Cuoco had plans that went beyond keeping horses. Having grown up around them, she was familiar with caring for animals. As the years passed, she began taking in different species, including animals that had been rescued from poor living conditions and horses that had retired from racing.By 2024, the property had become an important part of both her animal rescue work and her family life.In interviews with People magazine that year, Cuoco spoke about the animals living there, the changes she had made to the ranch and why providing older animals with a safe home meant so much to her.One of the unusual features of Cuoco's property is that several different species share the same living areas. Rather than keeping every type of animal completely separate, she has created spaces where smaller farm animals can live together.These include goats, pigs, chickens, ducks, miniature horses and dwarf ponies. Cuoco said the animals gradually establish their own relationships and become comfortable sharing the space."We have a big area where most of the little animals go, the goats, pigs, chickens and mini horses, and they all live together," she said.In the same interview, she revealed that two turkeys had recently joined the ranch. She had wanted to rescue turkeys for some time and was delighted by how friendly the birds were.The property also houses cows, including two named Connie and Ronnie, as well as donkeys and larger horses. Some of the horses are Thoroughbreds that have finished their racing careers.Cuoco has made changes to the property to accommodate its growing animal population. These include building a petting zoo and developing the barn, where she has also installed contemporary chandeliers.Not every animal arriving at Cuoco's ranch is young or healthy. Some have experienced difficult circumstances before being rescued, while others are already in the later stages of their lives.Cuoco has said that watching these animals settle into their new surroundings is one of the most rewarding parts of running the ranch. She particularly values being able to care for older animals that may have fewer years left to live."We have taken animals out of terrible situations, and to see the growth in how they thrive here, they’re all so happy," she said.Her interest in animal rescue is also connected to her experience with dogs. Cuoco previously had a rescued pit bull mix named Norman, who died in 2021.She has named both her production company and her pet-care brand after him. The brand, Oh Norman!, sells products including dog bowls, treats, toys and clothing. Cuoco has said she wanted a portion of purchases to support animal rescue organisations.While Cuoco initially developed the ranch around her interest in animals, it has also become a place where she wants her daughter, Matilda, to grow up learning about them. She said she introduced her daughter to the horses when she was very young and had even kept a pony for her to ride when she became old enough.However, Cuoco does not consider riding essential. She believes that simply spending time around animals, helping care for them, and understanding their routines can be valuable experiences for a child.Cuoco shares Matilda with actor Tom Pelphrey, whom she began dating in 2022. Pelphrey also shares her interest in animals. Cuoco recalled that his photographs with a German shepherd had caught her attention before their relationship began. When he first visited the ranch, he was surprised by what she had created there.The property has since become a place where the couple and their daughter spend time together, away from Cuoco's work in the entertainment industry.Despite having a large collection of rescued animals, Cuoco has spoken about one species she would particularly like to add to the ranch. In the 2024 interview, she also said that rescuing a giraffe remained an ambition she had not yet fulfilled. "I am still dying to rescue a giraffe. We have not done that yet," she said.Cuoco has owned several California properties during her acting career, including homes in Sherman Oaks, Tarzana, Hidden Hills and Agoura Hills.
Article Summary: Kaley Cuoco bought a 40-acre property in California for $4.99 million in 2017. Nine years later, the ranch has become a refuge for rescued animals. This includes horses, cows, goats, pigs, donkeys and birds. Cuoco has made changes to the property to accommodate its growing population.

Article Title: A fourth-generation Wisconsin farmer says a proposed $900 million power line could run within 300 feet of his home or cross 120 acres of his family's 2,500-acre cattle operation; the family is now fig
Article Text:
Why the transmission line is facing opposition

Legal battle moves into a critical phase

A proposed high-voltage transmission line in western Wisconsin has become the focus of a growing dispute between rural landowners and energy developers, with farmers warning that the project could reshape their properties and the surrounding landscape. According to the VernonReporter, the Coalition Against MariBell 765 has expanded its legal challenge, while Wisconsin Public Radio and local broadcaster WIZM News have also reported on residents’ concerns about land use, property values and the project's potential impact on the Driftless region. At the centre of the dispute is the proposed MariBell Transmission Project, a roughly 140-mile electricity corridor linking Marion, Minnesota, with Bell Center, Wisconsin. Developed by Dairyland Power Cooperative and GridLiance Heartland, the project would carry electricity at 765 kilovolts and 161 kilovolts using large steel transmission structures. For fourth-generation farmer Timothy J. Woodhouse and his extended family, the debate is about more than new infrastructure. It concerns the future of a cattle operation built across generations, and whether the proposed route could permanently alter the land on which the family lives and works.According to the coalition's amended court complaint, one proposed route would pass within 300 feet of Woodhouse's home. An alternative could cut through 120 acres of cropland and pasture belonging to the family's 2,500-acre operation. The family is not alone in its opposition. The coalition has also identified the farm of Larry Pedretti, Woodhouse's uncle and a third-generation farmer, as directly affected by both proposed routes. Pedretti raises beef cattle and uses a pacemaker and defibrillator, adding another layer to the family's concerns about working around the proposed high-voltage infrastructure. The lawsuit argues that the project could interfere with agricultural operations, damage property values and affect the rural environment. It also raises concerns about noise, electromagnetic fields and possible risks to human and livestock health. These are allegations made by the plaintiffs and have not been established as findings by a court.The MariBell project forms part of a wider effort to modernise the electricity network across the Upper Midwest. According to the developers' official project website, the proposed line would replace an existing 161-kilovolt transmission line with a double-circuit system capable of carrying electricity at 765 and 161 kilovolts.The developers say the upgrade would strengthen grid reliability, improve access to energy resources and help meet future electricity demand. They also plan to use existing transmission corridors where possible to limit the project's footprint. The proposed structures are expected to stand between 150 and 200 feet tall, with a right-of-way potentially extending up to 250 feet wide.However, residents have questioned whether the benefits justify the disruption to their communities. Wisconsin Public Radio has previously reported that some landowners are concerned about losing usable farmland, changes to the landscape and the possibility that the infrastructure will serve broader regional needs without providing direct connections to the communities along its route. Dairyland Power has said the project is not specifically designated to supply data centres.The dispute also comes amid broader agricultural concerns. On October 14, the Wisconsin Farm Bureau Federation said its preliminary analysis indicated that more than 3,000 of its member landowners could be directly affected by the MariBell and separate BECI transmission projects. The organisation warned that the combined developments could have significant consequences for farming and agribusiness across southern Wisconsin.The Coalition Against MariBell 765 filed its initial lawsuit against Dairyland Power Cooperative and GridLiance Heartland in May 2026, seeking to prevent the project from proceeding. In September, it submitted an amended complaint adding Woodhouse and Pedretti as individual plaintiffs and detailing the potential effects on their farms.The legal challenge is unfolding before the developers' anticipated application to the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity. The project website lists the fourth quarter of 2026 as the expected filing period. The commission's review will consider the project's need, costs, environmental effects and proposed routes, with opportunities for public participation.Opposition has meanwhile expanded beyond the courtroom. More than 100 landowners, farmers and public officials attended a rally in Genoa on October 12, organised by the coalition. The gathering was followed by a day of advocacy at the Wisconsin State Capitol, where residents pressed lawmakers to address the proposed transmission developments.For the Woodhouse family, the stakes remain deeply personal. The proposed line could bring towering electrical infrastructure close to their home or take productive acreage out of their farming operation. As the regulatory process advances, their legal fight reflects a wider question confronting rural communities: how to balance the need for a modern electricity grid with the rights of families whose land may be permanently changed by its expansion.
Article Summary: Coalition Against MariBell 765 has expanded its legal challenge. At the centre of the dispute is the proposed MariBell Transmission Project. It would link Marion, Minnesota, with Bell Center, Wisconsin. Developers say the upgrade would strengthen grid reliability. But residents question whether the benefits justify the disruption.

Article Title: Meet Dev Rai, the Indian-American Virginia student who founded a nonprofit at 15 to help artisans in India; two years later, it has supported over 400 craftspeople, sold 900 products and mobilised 300
Article Text:
Dev Rai founded a nonprofit at 15; it has helped 400 artisans, sold 900 products and mobilised 300 volunteers (Image Credit: Serving Society)

How a visit to India inspired the initiative

Connecting artisans with American buyers

Mobilising young volunteers across states

Balancing school with nonprofit work

Aiming for greater independence for artisans

At 15, while many teenagers are focused on school and extracurricular activities, Dev Rai established a nonprofit to help traditional artisans in India reach more customers. Two years later, his initiative, Serving Society Global Foundation, has raised more than $15,000, supported over 400 artisans, sold more than 900 handcrafted products and mobilised over 300 young volunteers. According to the organisation’s official website, its work combines support for economically disadvantaged communities with environmental sustainability and cultural preservation. Based in Virginia, the initiative connects Indian craft traditions with American buyers, while giving young volunteers opportunities to develop leadership, business and communication skills.Rai, an Indian-American student at Oakton High School in Virginia, founded Serving Society Global Foundation in 2024. The idea emerged from his visits to India, where he encountered artisans producing intricate handmade goods but struggling to secure consistent access to markets and recognition for their work. In an interview with FFXnow published on August 10, 2026, Rai explained that he saw an opportunity to introduce these products to American communities. He wanted to combine his interest in entrepreneurship and storytelling with his appreciation for Indian art and his desire to create a measurable social impact.Rather than starting from scratch, Rai reached out to nonprofit and government-supported organisations in India that were already working with artisans. These partnerships helped the foundation source handcrafted products and bring them to buyers in the United States.Serving Society focuses on helping artisans gain exposure beyond their immediate markets. Its products are introduced to customers through temples, cultural festivals, community events, grocery stores and other partner locations. The foundation’s official website reports that it has raised more than $15,000 for over 400 marginalised artisans and sold more than 900 items through eight local partner locations. The products include culturally inspired goods and environmentally conscious items, allowing the organisation to promote traditional craftsmanship while encouraging more sustainable consumption.The initiative aims to do more than sell individual products. By creating a route to American customers, it seeks to help artisan communities generate income and bring greater visibility to skills and designs passed down through generations. The foundation also supports the promotion of underrepresented cultures. Its model brings handmade products into everyday community spaces, giving customers opportunities to discover the people and traditions behind them.One of the initiative’s most significant developments has been its expansion among students. What began as a small project has grown into a network with seven chapters, 18 youth leaders and more than 300 volunteers, according to the foundation and FFXnow. Many volunteers are associated with the SEWA DC Youth Group. Students have helped with product sales, events and outreach, while social media and networking have helped the organisation attract participants beyond its original local base. Young people from Maryland, New Jersey, Minnesota and other parts of Virginia have expressed interest in establishing or leading chapters.Rai told FFXnow that he was surprised by how readily other students took ownership of the mission. Volunteers have progressed from helping at events to proposing ideas and leading activities of their own. The experience has also shaped his approach to leadership. Instead of managing every task himself, he has learned to delegate responsibilities and create opportunities for others to contribute.Running a growing organisation while attending high school requires careful planning. Rai told FFXnow that he tries to complete many projects during the summer, when students have fewer academic commitments. During the school year, he prioritises urgent tasks, breaks larger projects into weekly goals and plans around school deadlines. Delegation has become an important part of keeping the foundation's work manageable and sustainable.The organisation also provides volunteers with practical experience in business, communication and leadership. By helping organise events and connect products with customers, students can learn how a community-focused initiative operates while contributing to a wider social goal.The foundation’s future plans extend beyond selling products on behalf of artisan groups. Rai wants to help these communities build their own digital infrastructure so they can showcase, market and sell their work directly to customers. The aim is to reduce reliance on intermediaries and give artisan organisations tools they can continue managing independently. Such systems could help them reach wider audiences while maintaining greater control over how their products are presented and sold.For Rai, the longer-term goal is also to build an organisation that continues developing young leaders, even after its founder and early volunteers move on from school. Serving Society Global Foundation illustrates how a student-led initiative can connect cultural preservation, entrepreneurship and community service. Its progress so far reflects both the demand for traditional handmade products and the willingness of young volunteers to contribute to a cause beyond their own communities.
Article Summary: Dev Rai, an Indian-American student at Oakton High School in Virginia, founded Serving Society Global Foundation in 2024. The initiative connects Indian craft traditions with American buyers. It has raised more than $15,000, supported over 400 artisans, sold more than 900 handcrafted products and mobilised over 300 young volunteers.

Article Title: Who is the next Republican nominee for US President? JD Vance expects 2028 endorsement; Trump says 'no'
Article Text:
Donald Trump, JD Vance

What Trump said about Vance

Vance expects Trump's backing but leaves room for a contest
